entries.title: Sophomore QB Jeremy Davis leads Perspectives past Rauner in his varsity debut
entries.summary: <p>Perspectives is one of the Public League’s established, quality football programs. Terry Jones has coached the Warriors since 2010 and led the team to the state playoffs five times, including the last two seasons.</p><p>But this year his offense is in the hands of an inexperienced sophomore quarterback, Jeremy Davis.</p><p>“We trusted [Davis] and saw him throughout the summer workouts,” senior receiver Michael Johnson said. “We knew he would be ready. He’s just a kid right now. He will develop more and be even better.”</p><p>It was a dynamic first varsity game for Davis, as he ran for two touchdowns and threw for one to lead Perspectives to a 21-20 win against visiting Rauner on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/08/20/high-school-football-scores-chicago-illinois" >Thursday</a>.</p><p>“I was just trying to lock in and put my team on the map,” Davis said.</p><p>Davis had 13 carries for 94 yards. His second touchdown run came after leaping for a high snap. He kept his composure and scampered seven yards to put the Warriors (1-0) ahead 21-14 with 8:38 left.</p><p>“I just saw green and ran it in,” Davis said.</p><p>Rauner (0-1) responded quickly, scoring two minutes later. Quarterback Aiden Robinson connected with freshman Bryan Pinson for a 42-yard TD. It was the Wildcats’ only pass attempt of the game.</p><p>Perspectives stopped the two-point conversion attempt to preserve the lead. The Warriors’ defense needed one more big stop on the final drive and came through, keeping Rauner out of field goal range.</p><p>“The key to our defense playing tough in those big moments is to always encourage your teammates,” Perspectives senior Damon Smith, a linebacker, said. “It is all built on trust and courage and the brotherhood. If we trust each other, we will trust what we can do together.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Jeremy is my boy and I believe in this whole team and coach Jones. We are going to ball out.”</p><p>Junior running back Ryden Carrasco had 12 carries for 103 yards, including a 62-yard TD run. entries.title: Cade Townsend is Cubs pitching's far future, but what's near future look like when starters hit free agency?
entries.summary: <p>Cade Townsend is a 21-year-old who’s been a pro ballplayer for all of two months.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ first-round draft pick from earlier this summer is already ranked as their No. 4 prospect, but he’s a long way from the majors, yet to play a minor league game as he gets his first taste of life in the organization.</p><p>“It’s unreal. I don’t think there’s another organization like it,” Townsend said Wednesday. “I told my agents the day before the draft, ‘Get me here, no matter what. This is where I want to be.’ You really see that now, and it’s cool to see the process of: How does every day work together? It’s really a family, and I really appreciate that.”</p><p>These are early days. But Townsend figures to be an important piece of the Cubs’ long-term pitching puzzle.</p><p>The Cubs have used quality starting pitching as part of their formula to earn baseball’s fifth-best record and position themselves for a deep October run, and the current discussion centers on who’s going to get the ball in Game 1 of a playoff series.</p><p>But the discussion will eventually pivot to just how different the staff could look past the end of this season.</p><p>The team’s entire at-this-moment rotation could soon be gone: lefties Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga and David Peterson and righties Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes are all set to hit free agency at the end of the season.</p><p>There are some wrinkles, of course. Boyd has a $15 million mutual option for next season on his contract, and Holmes has a $12 million player option. But both pitchers have performed well enough — each making their case for that Game 1 start — that they’d figure to seek a raise in free agency.</p><p>There’s also the still-sizable pile of pitching injuries affecting guys who could make up a reasonably exciting starting group in 2027 and beyond. Righties Edward Cabrera, Ben Brown and Cade Horton, as well as lefty Justin Steele, are all on the injured list but under contract for next season.</p><p>Could it be a full-scale line change this offseason?</p><p>Certainly there would be plenty of questions about building a rotation entirely of guys coming off injuries of varying significance, including some that by next spring will have kept guys out for whole seasons.</p><p>Jed Hoyer’s front office could go to work in the winter and add to this group in free agency, even bringing some of their free-agents-to-be back, should they so desire.</p><p>Does it cast sort of a “Last Dance” feel on the home stretch and playoffs this season? The idea that this is the time to win with these pitchers? Boyd, Imanaga, Gausman and Holmes, if the season ended today, would seem to be the Cubs’ best options to form a postseason rotation. Come October, all four could be in their final days with the team.</p><p>Much further down the road than the start of next season, there’s Townsend, who represents a future wave of Cubs pitching.</p><p>The team liked the Ole Miss product enough to spend the No. 23 pick on him in this summer’s draft, despite his 6-foot-0 height, something the young righty knows has been mentioned as a potential hurdle to big league success.</p><p>He doesn’t see it that way and has opted to wear a rebuttal right on the back of his uniform.</p><p>“I’m actually wearing the No. 65,” Townsend said. “A lot of people said, ‘Man, you’re just a 6-foot right-hander.’ And when I’m on the mound, I think I’m 6-[foot]-5. I really think I’m better than you in every way.</p><p>“I don’t care how tall I am. Look at [Red Sox pitcher and 14-year major league veteran] Sonny Gray. He’s 5-[foot]-10, and he’s played a long time.”</p><p>Cubs fans can hope to see No. 65 on the mound at Wrigley Field someday, when there will surely be more changes on the pitching staff, the nature of the sport.</p><p>But the changes could be significant as soon as next year, before Townsend arrives, before Townsend even throws a pitch in a minor league game, perhaps.</p><p>The championship-level expectations the Cubs carry don’t figure to go away with a few free-agent arms this winter. Can the next wave keep the realistic World Series hopes alive?</p>

entries.title: Photos: the Illinois State Fair in Springfield
entries.summary: <p>The Illinois State Fair is a barrage to the senses. People squeal as they sit upside down on an amusement park ride, the smell of fried Oreos, funnel cakes and corn dogs waft in the air — and people parade through The Coliseum with their prized barrows, goats and steers. The annual fair, which is held in Springfield and runs until Aug. 26 this year, showcases the state's agricultural and livestock industry. It is both a tradition and a quintessential Midwest experience.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Man charged in South Shore shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man is facing attempted murder charges in connection with a Tuesday shooting in South Shore, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Marquise Earskines, 25, faces a charge for attempted murder and aggravated battery while discharging a firearm, along with a misdemeanor count of domestic battery, police said.</p><p>The 27-year-old man Earskines is alleged to have shot was in the 7300 block of South Blackstone Avenue at 8:43 p.m. when the two began arguing, and Earskines is alleged to have shot him in the left arm, police said. </p><p>The man was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center in critical condition.</p><p>Earskines was arrested less than an hour later, police said. He’s due in court for a detention hearing Friday.</p>

entries.title: Chicago police officer who racked up most complaints now faces firing — in two cases
entries.summary: <p>After racking up more complaints than any other Chicago police officer in recent years, Joseph Vecchio now faces firing in two of the disciplinary cases tied to his work on a notorious downtown tactical team.</p><p>Vecchio was among three members of the Near North District’s 1863 tactical team who had cases before the Chicago Police Board on Thursday, when members ruled on disciplinary disputes between the police department and the Civilian Office of Police Accountability.</p><p>The two cases seeking Vecchio’s dismissal relate to broader allegations that the unit had a pattern of conducting improper traffic stops. Vecchio was suspended for<b> </b>15 days in a third case, and the other tactical officers were also given significant suspensions.</p><p>Vecchio was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/01/16/chicago-police-cpd-joseph-vecchio-misconduct-discipline-complaints-lawsuit-snelling-traffic-stop" target="_blank" >stripped of his policing powers</a> late last year after COPA chief LaKenya White alerted former Supt. Larry Snelling to a “concerning number of complaints.”</p><p>“When COPA’s Policy, Research, and Development Unit conducted an analysis of complaint data since 2019, it revealed that Officer Vecchio has the highest number of log number investigations in the entire Department,” White wrote to Snelling on Oct. 6, 2025.</p><p>“Although many of these cases are still under investigation, the increasing number of complaints against Officer Vecchio suggests the need for immediate intervention by CPD.”</p><p>An attorney for Vecchio couldn't immediately be reached.</p><p>The cases announced by the police board on Thursday show the 1863 tactical team’s pattern of misconduct. Both of Vecchio’s cases involved searches that were apparently spurred by revelations that a car’s occupant had a gun license.</p><p>On Christmas 2024, Vecchio and another tactical officer approached a BMW parked in a loading zone with hazard lights on. They demanded the man seated in the passenger seat hand over his license, according to the police board ruling.</p><p>When Vecchio ran the license, he found the man had a license to own a gun, but not one to carry a gun publicly. He ordered the man out of the car, searched it and found a firearm in the center console, the ruling says.</p><p>But on the arrest report, both officers said they saw the man pull an L-shaped object from his waistband and reach toward the center console, prompting the search, according to the ruling.</p><p>Vecchio repeated this claim during a preliminary court hearing in the criminal case, which was later dropped by the Cook County prosecutors.</p><p>Snelling argued against any discipline but he was overruled by the board, which adopted COPA’s recommendation to fire Vecchio.</p><p>Arlette Porter, the board member who issued the ruling, said body camera footage showed there was “no reasonable articulable suspicion” the man they stopped was committing a crime.</p><p>“Officer Vecchio’s intentional inaccuracies, untruths, and misleading testimony before the Court was egregious and in direct contravention to CPD policy regarding honesty and accountability,” Porter wrote.</p><p>IIn Vecchio’s other dismissal case, stemming from a similar traffic stop, Snelling backed COPA’s push to have Vecchio fired but disagreed with recommendations for his partner.</p><div class="RelatedList police traffic stops plunge, again, but Black and Latino drivers still get pulled over far more</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" entries.title: Expect Todd Blanche to stay consistent with his dishonesty
entries.summary: <p>Todd Blanche was Donald Trump's personal attorney, so it was natural that when he was elevated to attorney general, a journalist asked whether he would "pledge that the Justice Department will always act independently of the White House?"</p><p>The correct answer to such a question is obvious: <i>The Justice Department and I are committed to the impartial administration of justice. We will always make prosecution decisions based solely upon the facts and the law after a fair evaluation of the evidence.</i></p><p>But Blanche said something a little different:</p><p>"No, I'm not going to pledge that. And no attorney general should ever pledge that. The president, I mean, if I were to pledge I will be independent of the White House, what that means is that if President Trump says, 'I want the Department of Justice to go after every violent criminal in this country,' which is what he has said, what you're saying to me is I should say, 'No, sir, I'm not going to do it.'"</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bd0000" name="module-bd0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>What jumps out first about Blanche's answer is the blithe refusal even to mouth (however disingenuously) the expected platitude. This is the Trumpian way. They don't just break the rules behind closed doors; they shatter the rules in broad daylight. It's not enough, for example, that the Trump Justice Department is denying resources to the team that investigates and prosecutes foreign corrupt practices; Donald Trump issued an executive order pausing all such prosecutions. So it's not news that Trump's new attorney general will fail to seek impartial justice, but the refusal to even feign regard for impartial justice is new.</p><p>The substance of Blanche's justification is also fatuous. Pledging to act independently of the White House doesn't mean acting in every instance in direct opposition to the president. That's absurd and it's not what independence requires. Nor could the president order the attorney general to "go after every violent criminal in this country," since more than 98% of violent crimes are state offenses, not federal ones, and in any case the combined forces of the state and federal governments don't have the resources to go after every violent criminal.</p><p>So much for deflection. The coffee-spitting moment came later, when Blanche was asked whether he would carry out an order that "crossed a legal or ethical line" and he proclaimed, "The president will never ask me to do something unethical or legal — or illegal. He never has. He never will."</p><p>Let's let the Freudian slip pass, but in fact the president had demanded that the Justice Department do something unethical <i>that very week</i> — namely, reconsider the decision to drop spurious vandalism charges against David Hearn. Jeanine Pirro's own motion to the court acknowledged that the original indictment was based upon false information provided by the Department of the Interior. Nevertheless, Trump fumed that Pirro had "choked." This week, we learned that she was convening a special grand jury for some unknown purpose. If I were Hearn, I'd keep my lawyer close.</p><p>And that perversion of justice is only a ripple in the flood of plainly politicized acts and forbearances by this administration. This is a president who sent a direct message to his attorney general demanding the prosecution of his political opponents. It's hard to think of how you could more comprehensively upend the idea of blind justice.</p><p>Trump's apologists do have a valid point when they note that the Manhattan district attorney's case against Trump in the Stormy Daniels case was also a form of lawfare. I said at the time that the case was flimsy and almost certainly would never have been brought if Trump were not the target. Trump's flagrant lawbreaking did present a quandary: How do you hold him responsible for his crimes without unintentionally validating the idea in the minds of his supporters that all justice is corruptly motivated?</p><p>There are no easy answers. Still, the Bragg prosecution was a local case, not the federal government seeking to punish a political foe. Ditto for the civil case Letitia James brought. At the federal level, Attorney General Merrick Garland was actually extremely reluctant to pursue federal charges against Trump despite the gravity of his conduct before and on Jan. 6. It was only after Trump announced his reelection bid that Garland felt compelled to appoint a special prosecutor (precisely to avoid the appearance of a conflict of interest).</p><p>Nor is it the case that President Joe Biden's administration used the Justice Department to settle political scores. To repeat, Garland was widely criticized for moving slowly against Trump's obvious lawbreaking in the Mar-a-Lago documents case as well as the Jan. 6 insurrection. One can understand his hesitation. One administration prosecuting another opens the possibility of a dangerous tit-for-tat, but whatever your view about the wisdom of going slow against Trump, it's preposterous to "whatabout" this. Under Garland's leadership, the department brought indictments against Rep. Henry Cuellar, Sen. Bob Menendez, Rep. T.J. Cox, Illinois Speaker Michael Madigan, Mayor Eric Adams (and we know how that turned out when Trump returned), Mayor Andrew Gillum and Hunter Biden — all Democrats.</p><h3>Along for Trump’s ride </h3><p>Trump's second-term Department of Justice, by contrast, has been a nonstop cavalcade of corruption, featuring blatantly political prosecutions, attempted prosecutions or investigations of Jerome Powell, Lisa Cook, Mark Kelly, Miles Taylor, Christopher Krebs, James Comey, "sandwich guy," Adam Schiff, Letitia James, Kilmar Abrego Garcia, Alex Padilla, John Brennan, John Bolton, Sean Dunn, Ras Baraka, Jacob Frey, anti-U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement protesters in Minnesota including the widow of Renee Good, and many more.</p><p>Biden made poor decisions in pardoning his family at the end, but that was trivial compared with the mass pardons for the Jan. 6 criminals, the pardons for cronies, donors, other corrupt public figures, the firings of any official who participated in the Jan. 6 or Mar-a-Lago investigations, the kid-glove treatment for Ghislaine Maxwell, and of course, the putrid attempt to create a $1.7 billion slush fund for so-called victims of lawfare along with a get-out-of-jail-free card for Trump and his insatiable family regarding past tax evasion.</p><p>The aptly named Blanche (because he should, but doesn't, blush) was along for all of it. He personally visited Maxwell in prison and has yet to provide an explanation for that highly unusual visit, nor for her promotion to a more comfortable prison. He was at the Department of Justice as 3,400 lawyers resigned in protest rather than engage in the kinds of unethical and unprofessional conduct Pam Bondi and Blanche were demanding. He has defended with a straight face James Comey's indictment for threatening the president with an Instagram photo of seashells.</p><p>This ethical flexibility was enough to make even some Republican senators hesitate about confirming him. But in the end, all but Susan Collins, of Maine, and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, voted yes, presumably because they fear that if it's not Blanche it will be someone even worse. Thus does Trump extort his party — by threatening to get even dirtier. But this tactic only succeeds because of learned helplessness by Republican office holders. In fact, when Trump gets pushback, he backs down. Ask Iran. Or consider the first utterly horrific attorney general candidate he proposed, Matt Gaetz. Enough Republicans balked that Trump withdrew his name. He didn't nominate someone even worse after that (admittedly a tall order). He went with Bondi, a smidge less awful.</p><p>It seems the tactic of standing up to Trump is just crazy enough to work. But, no, the GOP has not learned that lesson. They've chosen spinelessness instead, and even after a decade of this, I still cannot understand why.</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of The Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-010000" name="module-010000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Marking a middle-age milestone while watching the country ungracefully grow old
entries.summary: <p>I am a bicentennial baby in the throes of perimenopause. Spirit of ‘76, baby.</p><p>The United States is a young democracy, and I am becoming, ahem, a woman of a certain age.</p><p>My social media feed alternates between the latest doomsday political scenario to vitamins promising to tame belly fat more stubborn than a toddler at bedtime.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f70000" name="module-f70000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>This is another turning-50 column from a woman reckoning with aging and body change. Like most women in their 20s, I chafed at plastic surgery. Never considered going under the knife or allowing needles in my cheekbones. Women should age gracefully, and what kind of contradiction would it be to claim feminism and fillers, I thought. Well, now I’m less judgmental, and it has nothing to do with the male gaze. So I tell myself. Aging is a blessing — and a reminder of fading youth, because I gain 10 pounds if I glance at a croissant.</p><p>Watching influencers be open about Botox in their 20s or tweens ruining their future skin for complex skin care routines is concerning. Because I came of age before the era of filters and ring lights, I feel a little less vulnerable to the perfection demanded via social media. I refrain from comparing myself to Instagram baddies. But sometimes when I look in the mirror, I am amazed at how much I’ve physically changed in a couple of years. Lines around the mouth. Puffy eyes. I’m too scared of surgery and absolutely reject copying the cartoonish <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/society/2025/nov/18/mar-a-lago-face-plastic-surgery" target="_blank" ><u>Mar-a-Lago face</u></a> favored by MAGA women in the limelight. But maybe a little Botox and subtle cheek plumping are the tonic I need.</p><p>Then I remember I’m lazy. You have to keep up that habit of injections or you’ll fade back to your true self. I have neither the time nor money for ongoing maintenance. Kinda why I don’t dye my hair. I’m holding out hope to become a silver fox. But the grays are uncooperative and wiry. Kinda like the new chin hairs I pull — one of my latest hobbies.</p><p>If I stop midsentence, the brain fog takes over like a Chicago summer thunderstorm. Don’t expect me to remember my thoughts. Our group chats share portable fan and eye cream recommendations. I complain about weighing the most I’ve ever been but still pour a second class of champagne to go with fried chicken. The bright side of this new phase is my friends and feed have language (hello, perimenopause!) to complain about interrupted sleep and irritability. <a class="Link" href="https://abcnews.com/GMA/Wellness/breaking-taboo-menopause-10-commonly-asked-questions-answered/story?id=112840806" target="_blank" >Halle Berry is speaking up about menopause</a> and advocating for Congress to spend more money on research. I follow <a class="Link" href="https://www.drsharonmalone.com/" target="_blank" >Dr. Sharon Malone</a> for advice on hormone therapy and tips for surviving this life chapter. <a class="Link" href="https://hms.harvard.edu/news/how-gaps-scientific-data-lead-gaps-care-aging-women" target="_blank" >Scant research</a> exists on perimenopause or menopause. Go figure.</p><p>As women speak up and name their issues to doctors and anyone else who will listen, it’s important to dismiss shame and to share life changes. At the same time, our country is changing, and it’s important to name those threats and rotten politics gnawing at democracy. I recently traveled to Washington, D.C., and drove by federal buildings flanked with American flags and the president’s face in celebration of 250 years.</p><p>I couldn't help but think of "Botched," the reality show where doctors try and fix plastic surgeries gone wrong.</p><p>Maybe it's not me who needs the glow-up.</p><p>Our country could use more than a corrective nip and tuck to reverse the deep cracks that keep settling in, disfiguring the dewy sheen of hope and promise.</p><p><i>Natalie Y. Moore is a senior lecturer at Northwestern University.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-550000" name="module-550000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Mayor's tenants rights ordinance is attempt to sway voters
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson's so-called <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/27/renters-protection-ordinances-mayor-brandon-johnson-aldermanic-opponents-dueling-versions-chicago-city-council" >Protecting Renters Ordinance</a> is a cynical effort to garner votes among those who are ignorant of economic realities.</p><p>Without a doubt, Chicago is experiencing a deplorable lack of affordable housing. But this proposed ordinance will increase the operating costs to large and small landlords alike without having any impact on the supply of new rental units. It is economically naive to believe that landlords will just absorb the substantial legal and relocation costs generated by this ordinance without adding in these costs when it’s time to decide on future rent increases.</p><p>I don’t think the mayor is unaware of how markets operate. I think he hopes that by the time these increased costs are passed on to renters he may have succeeded in his reelection bid.</p><p><i>Mark Kaulas, Edgewater</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-290000" name="module-290000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Half-hearted enthusiasm won’t keep Bears in Illinois</h3><p>I have been a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" >Bears</a> fan since the 1960s. I’m looking forward to the upcoming season with great enthusiasm. I must say that the continuous banter about future stadium plans is getting very nauseating. The Bears are a business in the extremely profitable NFL. As a business, the franchise is seeking to build a new stadium that will benefit the organization. They purchased land in Arlington Heights to achieve that goal. The state Legislature, the city of Chicago and the governor have done little to nothing to ensure construction of a new stadium in Illinois, so Indiana saw an opportunity to try and lure the Bears away.</p><p>Unlike Illinois, Indiana sees a great business opportunity by building a new stadium. A new domed stadium could have other uses than hosting regular and postseason NFL games. It could host NCAA Final Fours, college football championships, Republican and Democratic conventions, etc.</p><p>The amenities at Soldier Field are not very fan-friendly. Chicago politicians keep claiming territorial ownership while fighting with the state Legislature on where the Bears should play. The land has been purchased. The location is favorable, with tollway access and public transportation. The land has potential to generate income for a state that could certainly benefit from it. Let’s hope the state Legislature can stop burying its heads in the sand and convince the Bears to build a new stadium in Arlington Heights before Indiana persuades them first.</p><p><i>Rick Kalin, Belmont Heights</i></p><h3>Perfect prose for our times </h3><p>I applaud Sun-Times reader Nathan Kempthorne for his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/08/15/cps-arts-south-west-business-reading-renters-trump-fauci-vaccines-birthright-steinberg-bey" >great letter/poem</a> on the state of the country under Donald Trump. It hit every nail on the head and was quite informative. He obviously hasn't been drinking the Trump Kool-Aid. Thank you, Mr. Kempthorne.</p><p><i>Richard Orrico, Melrose Park</i><br></p>

entries.title: America needs to get its priorities straight
entries.summary: <p>Last month in Nashville, at the National Urban League Conference, I delivered the 2026 State of the Urban League address with a simple message: America is facing a crisis of priorities.</p><p>As our nation celebrates its 250th anniversary, we should be asking whether the American Dream is becoming more attainable or slipping further out of reach.</p><p>For too many Americans, the answer is obvious.</p><p>Housing costs have skyrocketed. Healthcare remains unaffordable for millions. Childcare strains family budgets. Young people wonder whether they'll ever be able to buy a home. Even Americans with good jobs often feel one unexpected expense away from financial trouble.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2d0000" name="module-2d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>This is not a crisis of resources. It is a crisis of priorities.</p><p>The United States remains the wealthiest nation in the world. We have the capacity to expand affordable housing, strengthen schools, improve healthcare access, modernize infrastructure, and create pathways to economic mobility. The question is not whether we can afford to make these investments. The question is why we so often choose not to.</p><p>Instead, our politics increasingly revolves around division, distraction and grievance. We spend more time fighting cultural wars than solving kitchen table problems. While families worry about rent, groceries and retirement security, too much of our public debate is focused anywhere but on the challenges that shape people's daily lives.</p><p>Americans deserve better.</p><p>They deserve leaders who place affordability ahead of ideology. They deserve policies that reward work, not simply wealth. They deserve a government focused on expanding opportunity rather than manufacturing outrage.</p><p>That's why the National Urban League continues to defend diversity, equity and inclusion against relentless political attacks.</p><p>The opponents of DEI have succeeded in turning a straightforward idea into a political buzzword. But stripped of the rhetoric, the principle is simple: Everyone deserves a fair shot.</p><p>Equal opportunity is not a threat to excellence. It is the foundation of excellence.</p><p>When qualified people are given the chance to compete, businesses grow stronger. When barriers are removed, communities prosper. When talent is cultivated wherever it exists, our economy becomes more innovative and competitive.</p><p>America has always moved forward by widening the circle of opportunity, not shrinking it.</p><p>The same principle applies to voting rights.</p><p>A democracy works best when participation is encouraged, not restricted. At a time when faith in public institutions is declining, the answer is not to make voting harder. The answer is to make civic participation stronger.</p><p>Throughout our history, every major expansion of democracy has made the nation more representative, more responsive and more just. We should be building on that progress, not reversing it.</p><p>But defending democracy and opportunity is only part of the challenge. We also must confront the affordability crisis squeezing working families in every corner of the country.</p><p>That means raising wages so that a full-time job provides genuine economic security. It means expanding affordable housing so families aren't forced to spend unsustainable portions of their income on rent. It means investing in workforce training and education so Americans can compete in a rapidly changing economy. It means ensuring affordable internet access so that no child, worker or entrepreneur is locked out of opportunity by the digital divide.</p><p>These are not partisan ideas. They are practical solutions.</p><p>The American people are less interested in ideological battles than they are in whether they can afford a home, save for retirement, start a business or send their children to college. They want an economy that works for them. They want a democracy that includes them. They want a future that looks brighter than the present.</p><p>As America enters its third century, we face a defining choice.</p><p>We can continue down a path of widening inequality, growing division and shrinking opportunity. Or we can recommit ourselves to the values that have always made this country stronger: democracy, inclusion and economic mobility.</p><p>Future generations will not judge us by the slogans we repeated or the partisan victories we claimed. They will judge us by whether we expanded opportunity, strengthened democracy and reduced poverty.</p><p>At 250 years old, America's promise remains as powerful as ever. But promise alone is not enough.</p><p>It's time to get our priorities straight. Because the true measure of our nation is not how much wealth it creates, but whether that prosperity reaches the people who need it most.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/marc-h-morial" target="_blank" ><i>Marc H. Morial</i></a><i> is president and CEO of the National Urban League</i> <i>and</i> <i>was mayor of New Orleans from 1994 to 2002.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-220000" name="module-220000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Friend Has Heavy Heart Over Woman's Weight Issues
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My friend of many years, whom I consider to truly be part of the family, has made food the only thing that makes her happy. Besides my husband, she's all I have left. She went to a doctor a couple years ago who told her she must lose weight, but she ended up gaining more.</p><p>I've tried talking to her, but she says I am preaching to the choir. It doesn't help that her husband is also obese. They enjoy eating out constantly. She has many physical things wrong with her, most of which could be helped greatly by losing at least 80 pounds.</p><p>I want to write her a letter and tell her how hard it is watching her kill herself by not trying to help herself. She has a heart problem, and the extra weight certainly is not helping it. She has several other problems, too. She has aches and pains everywhere — her knees hurt, her feet hurt and her liver is not doing well from all the medications. Getting rid of most of the excess weight would definitely help her get around and make her healthier. It most likely would even get her off some of the medications.</p><p>I wish I could write her and tell her that her daughter, son, husband, brother, sister-in-law, and especially her 7-year-old granddaughter and I really need her and want her to be around. Talking to her doesn't help, so do you think a letter would be inappropriate? — <i>STATING MY CASE IN IDAHO</i></p><p><b>DEAR STATING:</b> I am going to assume that you have already told this friend all the things you have in your letter to me. I am not sure how helpful it would be to put those thoughts in a letter. Your friend and her husband have a ritual they practice together — eating out. Unless both of them are willing to recognize it is causing serious health problems and are willing to do something about it, nothing will change.</p><p>There is a group that has been mentioned in this column many times called Overeaters Anonymous. It is a self-help group with a long and successful history. In these meetings there is no weighing, no shaming, no dues or fees for members. (They are self-supporting through their own contributions.) While it might not be something your friend is willing to explore, it might make you feel better to suggest this to her if she's unaware of it. The website is oa.org.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My mother has accused me of removing personal papers from her file cabinet. I have never gone into her file cabinet, nor have I ever removed any papers. This accusation is extremely hurtful. It has strained our relationship. I place great emphasis on honesty and integrity. I am now considering taking a polygraph test to validate my defense. Should I follow through or just let it go? — <i>HONEST DAUGHTER</i></p><p><b>DEAR DAUGHTER:</b> Let it go. A polygraph test has a wide margin of error, so it wouldn't provide conclusive proof anyway. Instead, try to understand that your mother's accusation may come from frustration with herself at having misplaced the papers. She was wrong to take it out on you, but please show that you can be more forgiving than she has been.</p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Many Trump-endorsed candidates landing with a thud
entries.summary: <p>On Tuesday night, Darline Graham, sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., revealed somewhat awkwardly that she is entirely unprepared to be a U.S. senator.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.nydailynews.com/2026/08/19/darlene-graham-debate-south-carolina-senate/" target="_blank" >At a South Carolina debate</a>, she was asked a perfectly reasonable and straightforward question: “Are Taiwan and the South China Sea national security issues for the United States?” And, “If so, why?”</p><p>She sheepishly responded, “I’m just going to be honest here — I’m not on national security. I’m not that informed on national security, but I do support the military.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-970000" name="module-970000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>That response — admitting there’s an entire and extremely important category of public policy and governing responsibility that she just doesn’t know — would be humiliating for any Senate candidate, but it was worse considering her brother’s personal interest and commitment to it.</p><p>It was also another reminder that President Donald Trump, who has lent considerable support to her candidacy, doesn’t care about qualifications, expertise or even electability when he backs candidates for public office. All that matters is loyalty.</p><p>This is not news. Whether it was his ill-fated support of scandal-ridden Senate candidates Herschel Walker and Roy Moore in 2022 and 2017 respectively, or of current scandal-ridden candidates Ken Paxton and Max Miller, Trump has endorsed some truly awful candidates, often betting that his word alone would be enough to push them across the finish line.</p><p>Walker and Moore excluded, he’s had a lot of success, to be sure, and in many cases his support was in fact what propelled otherwise lackluster or problematic candidates to victory. But this primary season has seen a mixed bag for Trump, begging the question of whether his golden touch has lost some of its shine — especially as his approval sinks to an abysmal 32%.</p><p>A string of recent losses show voters aren’t entirely sold on Trump’s vision for the next two years.</p><p>This week, scandal-ridden Rep. Cory Mills, R-Fla., lost his primary in Florida, as did Catalina Lauf.</p><p>Megan Degenfelder lost her bid for governor in Wyoming, while election-denier Mike Lindell lost his primary for governor in Minnesota by 11 points.</p><p>Earlier this month, Trump-backed gubernatorial candidates in Iowa and Georgia also lost, as did his first pick for governor of South Carolina.</p><p>Altogether, 10 Trump-endorsed candidates have lost their primaries, which are as many losses as Trump saw in 2018, 2020 and 2024 combined. One more loss and he’ll tie his worst record for endorsements, in 2022.</p><p>With the fight over the majority at stake, it seems an odd year to be so capricious and reckless with his influence, but capricious and reckless he’s been.</p><p>In Texas, Trump endorsed Paxton, whose <a class="Link" href="https://www.thebarbedwire.com/ken-paxton-scandal-timeline/" target="_blank" >20-year record</a> of scandals, including a felony securities fraud indictment and an impeachment by his own party, baffles the mind when the well-liked incumbent John Cornyn was also on the ballot.</p><p>In Ohio, Miller has been accused by his ex-wife and father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, of spousal and child abuse, and yet Trump has not demanded he step down. The White House even <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/10/white-house-max-miller-pressure-campaign-01031353" target="_blank" >reportedly</a> pressured Ohio Republicans to lay off Miller.</p><p>In the hotly watched races where Trump’s picks have lost, it means Republican primary voters in red states like Iowa, Florida and Wyoming — in other words, Trump’s base — are either tuning Trump out or proactively voting against his candidates. Both scenarios are bad for Republicans, especially in the cases where his more controversial candidates, like Paxton and Miller, have to run in a general election.</p><p>We know Trump’s lost massive support among independents, young voters, Hispanics and other coalitions from 2024. But if he can’t turn his base out for his candidates as reliably as he once did, well add it to the pile of reasons Democrats feel pretty good about these midterms — and hope he keeps backing all the bad contenders he wants.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e40000" name="module-e40000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: After their dad was deported, family works to keep his Chicago sandwich shop and legacy alive
entries.summary: <p>Nooran Amin knows the drill by now at the Best Sub #2 sandwich shop in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/humboldt-park" >Humboldt Park.</a></p><p>On a stiflingly hot weekday morning, he opens the door, heads toward the kitchen and turns on the grill and the deep fryers.</p><p>“Those two things take the longest to heat up,” he says. “Then, I turn on the lights, turn on the fans, take some fries out, take the burger buns out.”</p><p>Nooran is 19. Until last fall, he was a college student at Dominican University who loved watching football and sending Instagram reels to his friends. He had a part-time job at an optical store near his family’s home in Addison and helped work the cash register at Best Sub #2 — his dad’s restaurant — only during school breaks.</p><p>Everything changed last September. That's when Nooran’s father, 64-year-old Asif Amin Cheema, was detained by federal immigration agents just three minutes from his home during the early days of Operation Midway Blitz. Despite having no criminal record, he was arrested because he had a removal order for a missed court date, something the family says their former immigration lawyer did not tell them about. </p><p>Since that day, the family has been trying to keep the sandwich shop afloat while settling into a busier — and decidedly harder — new life without their patriarch. And as the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign continues to upend the lives of families throughout the United States, they wonder whether the country where Cheema built his life still welcomes them.</p><p>When the family learned Cheema was in detention at the Broadview ICE facility, Nooran, the youngest of five kids, was given his marching orders.</p><p>“They were, like,’You're gonna have to take care of the store, you're gonna have to step up,’ ” he says.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Nooran Amin, 19, is helping to run his father’s sandwich shop. He’s had to take on a lot more responsibility since his father was deported back to Pakistan.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Esther Yoon-Ji Kang/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Stepping up</h3><p>Nooran’s dad spent close to three months in detention at the Clay County Jail in Indiana. He lost 30 pounds and experienced various health complications.</p><p>On New Year’s Day this year, he was <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2026/02/09/chicago-area-asians-were-arrested-in-midway-blitz-for-a-while-they-kept-quiet-about-it?subscription=true" target="_blank" ><u>deported</u></a> to Pakistan, a place where he hadn't lived for more than 30 years.</p><p>Nooran, whose facial hair does little to hide his baby face, had to learn the ins and outs of the shop from an employee, a family friend he calls “Uncle.”</p><p>Now, he opens and closes the sub shop by himself many days and is even trying to modernize the place. He replaced a cash register that was older than he is for a new electronic system that tracks popular items and the restaurant's busiest times. He’s thinking of new menu items to help with sales.</p><p>There’s a lot less time for watching sports, playing cricket and seeing friends.</p><p>When asked if he misses his old life, Nooran answers with a soft “yeah.”</p><p>He recently transferred to the architecture program at the University of Illinois Chicago, and he’s not sure how he’ll juggle school and the sandwich shop. But he has to make it work because his mother and siblings are all busy with other responsibilities.</p><p>“I don't want to put more pressure on them,” he says. “If I can’t do it, then who will?”</p><p>When Nooran’s dad was first detained, he told the family to sell the sub shop so it wouldn’t be a burden. But that was never an option, according to the Amin children.</p><p>“If we lose this restaurant, we'll lose anything of my dad in the U.S.,” Nooran says.</p><p>His sister, Rabia Amin, agrees. So she’s grateful that her baby brother — whom she still remembers as a pudgy, grumpy toddler — took the reins at the shop.</p><p>“I’m really proud of him, and I tell him this,” says Rabia, 27. “He's had to build a lot more confidence [and] take a lot more responsibilities than he probably should have at his age.”</p><p>Rabia, too, has a packed schedule, working as a law clerk downtown and studying for the bar exam. She helps with the business side of the sandwich shop and is keeping up with her dad’s immigration case. When heavy rains flood the family’s basement, Rabia is on cleanup duty, too.</p><p>A self-proclaimed “unserious person,” Rabia is quick to crack a joke or get loud and animated. But when asked how the family is coping, she suddenly chokes up and reaches for a tissue.</p><p>Some days, she will come home from work and see her mother crying. The late-night FaceTime calls with her dad aren’t always easy because everyone is tired from their long days.</p><p>She says “it takes 20 people” to fill the void her father has left. While she has tried to help everyone get out of the house more and practice self-care, the family is still in survival mode, with every member carrying a heavier load, living busier than ever.</p><p>Except for her dad, back in the village he left as a young man.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a He had not lived there in more than 30 years.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Alone in Pakistan</h3><p>“I still don't think he's accepted the fact that he's in Pakistan,” Rabia says.</p><p>She visited him in April, for his birthday, taking some of his medicine and clothes over.</p><p>She says Cheema — who used to work 12-hour days and then would come home to garden, spend time with his family, and care for his beloved pet birds — looked lethargic and took a lot of naps, something he rarely did here.</p><p>Rabia recalls a plaintive moment during that trip in April, when Nooran FaceTimed his dad from the sandwich shop to ask a question about a malfunctioning deep-fryer. Cheema talked his son through the steps to fix it, and the fryer was up and running in no time.</p><p>But then, Rabia says, he grew quiet and “started disassociating.” She asked him what was wrong and gently coaxed a response out of him.</p><p>“He basically was like, ‘It just made me really sad seeing him working there and me not being there. I miss the restaurant, I miss my son, I miss my wife. Why am I here?’ ” Rabia recalls. “I've never seen my dad like that ever.”</p><p>Rabia says her dad missed several big milestones in his kids’ lives in the past year: Her little sister, who the siblings agree is their dad’s favorite child, graduated from college. Her older sister got engaged. And, of course, there were the parties and family gatherings where he used to be a boisterous and larger-than-life presence.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div She says he has been lethargic and unmotivated because his family is not with him.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Esther Yoon-Ji Kang/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3> ‘I don’t think this country is deserving of my father’</h3><p>Cheema recently bought a flock of pigeons to take care of in the village. Rabia is not fond of them, but they bring her dad some joy. The family has encouraged him to start a sandwich shop in the village, but he has been resistant. Rabia thinks that’s because his family, his biggest source of motivation, is not with him.</p><p>She says she is beginning to accept that her dad will never be the same again. And now, she’s worried about him aging in Pakistan by himself.</p><p>“I wanted to be the one who took care of my parents when they got old. That's what me and my siblings always planned,” she says. “I don't know if I can do that because dad is across the world right now.”</p><p>She’s also been feeling a lot of guilt lately.</p><p>“Dad gave up everything and gave me such a beautiful life,” she says. “I have a dream job, I have a dream house. My family's great, my friends are amazing … and Dad's just back where he left.”</p><p>Recently, the family started exploring the idea of moving to another country, like Canada or England. They haven’t thought through all the details, but the idea is to relocate to a place where everyone can travel freely without fear.</p><p>They’ll still see if there’s a way to bring Cheema back to the U.S., but they’ve tried unsuccessfully to get him legal status here before, and the process is long.</p><p>Moreover, Rabia says, the family has been feeling less welcome in America these days.</p><p>“Why would you not want a hard-working, successful businessman who raised five kids here who all contribute to society?” she says. “I don't think this country is deserving of my father, or entries.title: Chicago’s Manasseh has a new album. It’s a tribute to his younger self
entries.summary: <p>Manasseh listened to Brandy’s 1994 debut on cassette so many times that the tape melted.</p><p>It was the first secular album the Chicago artist was allowed to own, a gift from his mother, Idella. Twenty-six years after her death, Manasseh still feels his mother’s presence on his upcoming sophomore album “R&B[eyond]” — out Tuesday, the day he turns 39.</p><p>“I would hear her sing all the time in the house; we would sing together,” he said. “When I’m singing, I’m having my lowest days, I really do feel like she’s hugging me.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div </div><p>Friday, Manasseh plans to celebrate the album’s release a few days early with <a class="Link" href="https://dice.fm/event/92kk7d-manasseh-birthday-show-featuring-hasani-cannon-w-abolishvictory-21st-aug-epiphany-center-for-the-arts-the-sanctuary-chicago-tickets" target="_blank" ><u>a performance at the Epiphany Center for the Arts</u></a>. </p><p>He’s joined by local artists <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/abolishvictory/" target="_blank" ><u>ABOLISHVICTORY!</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/realhasanicannon/" target="_blank" ><u>Hasani Cannon</u></a>. For the artist, whose given name is Manasseh Croft, the album is a long time coming and is his most personal project to date. </p><p>Growing up attending a West Englewood Baptist church, Manasseh was raised on gospel music. He would catch snippets of mainstream artists on the radio, but then the Brandy tape opened the door to TLC, Britney Spears, Blackstreet, the Spice Girls, “VH1 Divas” and eventually his own music career.</p><p>“I really, really am so grateful for her allowing me to dive into that,” he said of his mom. “She did me the biggest favor back in the ‘90s by giving me that tape.”</p><div The album is an ode to the permission his mother gave him to embrace secular music, but it’s also a tribute to his younger self. Its cover shows a 7-year-old Manasseh, clad in a purple button-down and blue patterned vest from the JCPenney husky section.</p><p>“I think it’s the best way I could show (my younger self) that I’m serious about our healing, about our growth and development, about the way we see ourselves,” he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d60000" name="image-d60000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ce15e15/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3080x1729+0+676/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8b%2Fb0%2Fc4940aa0460385cb3bb9fb546c5b%2F0-manasseh-r-beyond-album-artwork.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/625aa19/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3080x1729+0+676/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8b%2Fb0%2Fc4940aa0460385cb3bb9fb546c5b%2F0-manasseh-r-beyond-album-artwork.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a79e49c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3080x1729+0+676/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8b%2Fb0%2Fc4940aa0460385cb3bb9fb546c5b%2F0-manasseh-r-beyond-album-artwork.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="0. Manasseh - R&B[eyond] album artwork.png" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a79e49c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3080x1729+0+676/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8b%2Fb0%2Fc4940aa0460385cb3bb9fb546c5b%2F0-manasseh-r-beyond-album-artwork.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/58961be/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3080x1729+0+676/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8b%2Fb0%2Fc4940aa0460385cb3bb9fb546c5b%2F0-manasseh-r-beyond-album-artwork.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a79e49c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3080x1729+0+676/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8b%2Fb0%2Fc4940aa0460385cb3bb9fb546c5b%2F0-manasseh-r-beyond-album-artwork.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The album cover of “R&B[eyond]” features a young Manasseh in his favorite outfit on picture day at Hope Lutheran Church and School. “That smile, that’s for real,” Manasseh recalled. “I never felt more beautiful than in that outfit.”</p></figcaption></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Recorded largely in friends’ living rooms — except the tracks “Todo” and “Right Now,” which came together at <a class="Link" href="https://www.studioshapeschicago.com/" target="_blank" ><u>studioSHAPES</u></a> — “R&B[eyond]” has a distinctly Chicago sound. It features about a dozen Chicago collaborators, including trumpeter <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/mhillsounds/" target="_blank" ><u>Marquis Hill</u></a>, rapper-professor <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/femdotdotcom/" target="_blank" ><u>femdot.</u></a>, musician and producer <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/marcussdarling/" target="_blank" ><u>Marcus Darling</u></a>, rapper <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FYQRbL5m1uQ" target="_blank" ><u>Heavy Crownz</u></a> and producer <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/renzell.wav/" target="_blank" ><u>Renzell</u></a>.</p><p>One standout track is <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=juK-naexxJI" target="_blank" ><u>“Junie,”</u></a> produced by Chicago-born <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/eddieburns/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>Eddie Burns</u></a> and featuring local R&B-rap artist <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/galaxyfrancis/" target="_blank" ><u>Galaxy Francis</u></a>. It’s a psychedelic soul-encased escape from reality, that ponders a new identity and a break from the weight of everyday life. The 13-track album also includes a phone-recorded cover of Roberta Flack’s 1974 classic “Feel Like Makin’ Love,” a spoken interlude and songs made back in 2022, wrapping up in a nine-minute jam session with hip-hop-jazz-soul band <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/leftjones_/" target="_blank" ><u>Leftjones</u></a>.</p><p>“This album is very much a culmination of where I’ve been and the things that I’ve wanted to do,” he said. “For the first time in a very long time, I’m so satisfied with what has been created. I think the biggest thing is I didn’t have to do it by myself.”</p><p>To Manasseh, the album isn’t just a collection of songs. It’s an act of catharsis.</p><p>“I just pray everyone that gets the chance to hear it feels lighter when it ends than when it started,” he said. “This is for the inner child in you. This album is for you, all of you, every stage of you.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago police failed to identify cop whose guns were found during FBI raid of felon’s home
entries.summary: <p>Did a Chicago cop hand over two guns to a now-convicted extortionist and then lie to the police department about what happened to them?</p><p>That explosive question arose in federal court filings in the case of Jawad Fakroune, a politically connected Chicago businessman who was convicted in June and is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/06/30/jawad-fakroune-federal-prosecutors-fbi-pritzker" target="_blank" >now serving a six-year prison sentence</a> for threatening a restaurant owner over a $1.5 million debt.</p><p>But the officer's identity still remains a mystery.</p><p>The Chicago Police Department’s Bureau of Internal Affairs opened an investigation into the matter but came up empty, according to records released in response to a Freedom of Information Act request. The Chicago Sun-Times was unable to independently identify the cop.</p><p>The gun mystery emerged in June 2025 as federal prosecutors fought to keep Fakroune locked up while he was awaiting trial. They argued that he posed a danger to the public.</p><p>Fakroune had gone on the run after being charged in late 2024 with extortion.</p><p>When FBI agents raided his New York apartment, they found two Glock handguns. But Fakroune was gone. He'd slipped away. He later was arrested at a home in northwest Indiana.</p><p>Fakroune's case attracted attention because of his relationships with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/01/20/extortion-chicago-pritzker-fbi-restaurants-phil-stefani-jawad-fakroune" target="_blank" >political and business figures</a> including <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/04/11/lisa-duarte-jawad-fakroune-jbpritzker-jb-pritzker-rahm-emanual-lobbying" >Lisa Duarte,</a> a former top aide to Gov. JB Pritzker, and Phil Stefani, a well-known Chicago restaurateur.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-3d0000" name="image-3d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" </div><p>To bolster his tough-guy reputation, Fakroune told people he was a son of Pablo Escobar, the Colombian drug lord who died in 1993.</p><p>According to prosecutors, a man they identified in court papers only as "Individual A" told federal investigators that he had left guns at one of Fakroune’s Chicago homes and never got them back.</p><p>Individual A identified the weapons as the same two Glocks recovered by the FBI in New York, prosecutors said. They said he had reported the guns stolen.</p><p>Then, in a failed bid to spring Fakroune on bail while he awaited trial, Damon Cheronis, his lawyer, dropped a bombshell: Individual A was a cop.</p><p>"Individual A is an admitted heavy drinker who, regarding the 'firearms,' walked into a police station and filed a false police report claiming the guns were stolen," Cheronis wrote. "This should give the court pause in relying on anything proffered by the government as it relates [to] Individual A."</p><p>Cheronis didn’t name the officer.</p><p>At the time, the Sun-Times asked the police department about the lawyer's revelation. But officials said they <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/06/20/jawad-fakroune-chicago-police-department-extortion" target="_blank" >didn’t know about the accusations</a>.</p><p>The internal affairs bureau then began an investigation into a possible violation of the police department's Rule 14, which prohibits officers from making false reports.</p><p>An investigator sent certified letters to Fakroune and Cheronis in July 2025, seeking information about the mystery cop. A lawyer for Fakroune responded that he couldn't disclose anything to the investigator.</p><p>The investigator also filed a Freedom of Information Act request with the FBI. But the FBI wouldn't cooperate. It responded that it could neither confirm nor deny information involving "confidential human sources."</p><p>The internal affairs bureau closed the case this February without identifying the officer.</p><p>"Without cooperation from the victim [Fakroune] or having any independent witnesses come forward to provide corroborating evidence, the Reporting Sergeant cannot proceed with this investigation," the internal affairs investigator told his bosses.</p><p>Fakroune was sentenced to prison in June. He's still facing trial in October on separate federal tax charges.</p><p>In response to a public records request, the police department released the internal affairs investigator’s reports but with parts blacked out.</p><p>Fakroune and his lawyer didn't respond to requests for comment. A police spokesperson declined to comment.</p><p>Last year, in an attempt to identify the officer, the Sun-Times reviewed reports filed by Chicago cops who said their guns had been stolen. None of those records appeared to match the circumstances described in Fakroune’s case.</p><p>So the identity of the cop known as Individual A — and the full story of how his Glocks wound up with a now-convicted extortionist — remain a mystery.</p><p><i>Contributing: Tim Novak</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://illinoisanswers.org/2026/04/10/chicago-cops-did-little-to-probe-gun-stolen-from-police-station/" target="_blank" >Chicago Cops Did Little to Probe Gun Stolen From Police Station and Used in Three Shootings, New Records Show</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/06/30/jawad-fakroune-federal-prosecutors-fbi-pritzker" target="_blank" >Man who posed as drug lord Pablo Escobar’s son gets 6 years in prison for ‘terrorizing’ Chicago business partner</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Mother Goose is getting a Natalie Merchant makeover
entries.summary: <p>Singer-songwriter Natalie Merchant has spent years as an international star — first with the band 10,000 Maniacs and then as a successful solo artist. But one of her biggest musical satisfactions has nothing to do with the big-stage limelight.</p><p>Merchant’s “Cabinet of Wonder,” a digital children’s album on the Nonesuch label, marks the culmination of an ongoing project she calls her “legacy.” It’s an ambitious educational collaboration with the Chicago Children’s Theatre and Chicago Symphony Orchestra that features an accompanying website with recordings, videos and teaching aids free for teachers, parents, children and anyone else.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" data-align-center> <div id="Form-newsletter-wrapper" target="_blank" >Privacy Policy</a></p> </div> </form> </bsp-form> </div> </div><p>The concept behind it all is simple. Merchant has set 14 Mother Goose nursery rhymes to music, using the familiarity and metrical patterns of the venerable texts combined with her catchy tunes to teach preschool and kindergarten-age children a love for both music and language.</p><p>“Children deserve beauty,” Merchant said, “and people who develop a sense of aesthetics at a really young age and who create beauty, make better citizens, make a better society, make a better world. So, in a small way, I am accomplishing the goals I have always had through music. I’ve always wanted to make the world a slightly better place for people.”</p><p>For the singer, “Cabinet of Wonder” is not just a vanity project. Instead of just donating a few hours of time, the singer-songwriter has thrown every ounce of her being into this effort.</p><p>She not only wrote all the songs, she performed for all of the music videos and album tracks, edited the videos with the post-production company, Abstrakt, and oversaw the creative direction of the album’s accompanying educational website, which launched last year. And if all that wasn’t enough, Merchant even designed and made all the costumes for the project.</p><p>“It is a very deep passion that she has for children and education and literature,” said Jacqueline Russell, co-founder and artistic director of the Chicago Children’s Theatre, and a friend of Merchant’s for nearly two-decades.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/1JwkRbVt5_g?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Natalie Merchant - Little Miss Muffet (Official Video)"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>It is easy to wonder if Mother Goose rhymes, which date back to the 18th century and beyond, still have relevance to children growing up in a world of social media, smart phones and video games. And according to Merchant, the answer is a resounding yes.</p><p>“I lived it for three years. I was in the field, and I know it works,” Merchant said of her time working with students in a Head Start preschool program near her home in upstate New York – a time when the seeds of “Cabinet of Wonder” were planted. “I know the joy it brings to the children. I know the joy it brings to the teachers, too.”</p><p>After the “Cabinet of Wonder” website launched in November 2025, CSO musicians and Children’s Theatre teaching artists took the songs to preschool and kindergarten students in a dozen partner Chicago public schools, with teachers prepping the youngsters and helping them learn the words.</p><p>Those students plus others up to grade 2 from schools citywide—3,000 in all—came to May 8 presentations of “Cabinet of Wonder” with Merchant and guest conductor James Bagwell at Orchestra Hall. Those two concerts were followed the next day by two paid family concerts that drew another 2,500 people.</p><p>“It was crazy how much the children loved the music,” Russell said. “It was like a rock concert. None of these children were staying in their seats. We were at Orchestra Hall but we could have been at the United Center with the amount of enthusiasm and cheering.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" preschool and kindergarten students in a dozen partner Chicago public schools.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Fábian Aguirre</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>While working at the Head Start program beginning in 2017, Merchant realized there was no arts programming for these preschoolers, so she started writing and teaching songs based on Mother Goose rhymes.</p><p>At the end of the COVID-19 pandemic, Merchant came to Chicago to mix an album at Electrical Audio, and she asked Russell to spend a day with her. The singer shared her experiences with the preschool students and played some of her Mother Goose tunes.</p><p>The Children’s Theatre has been partners for about 15 years with the CSO, and its educational arm, the Negaunee Institute, on the family series, “Once Upon a Symphony.” They had also done some on-line video productions during the pandemic and wanted to do more that could take their work beyond Chicago.</p><p>“Suddenly, I thought this might be that project,” Russell said.</p><p>So, in the Spring 2023, she set up a meeting with the Negaunee Institute’s Jonathan McCormick. He was aware of Merchant’s artistry and was intrigued to hear of her work in Troy, N.Y.</p><p>“Then, to sit with her in person and hear directly what that experience meant to her, we were hooked,” he said. “We saw the ingredients for something really special — Natalie’s vision, the Children’s Theatre’s aesthetic and collaborative abilities and what we could offer musically to it.”</p><p>The first thing they wanted to do was create the website that teachers and others would use to learn the songs and teach them. After several rounds of discussion, it was decided that “Cabinet of Wonder” would comprise the 14 Mother Goose tunes and three additional original songs — two that introduce the series and another that concludes it.</p><p>At the same time, Merchant worked with one of the members of her touring band, violinist Megan Gould, to create chamber versions of her songs, using instruments from across the orchestra. In all, 22 different musicians — members of the CSO and guest artists — recorded the songs. They’re prominently featured in the videos with 25 child actors, often wearing costume headpieces.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure bebop groove of “Jack Sprat.”</p><p>“We wanted kids to get all the flavors we could possibly fit in there,” Merchant said.</p><p>In 2026-27, the CSO and Children’s Theatre will expand their CPS At the same time, Merchant is teaming with the National Head Start Association to lead teacher training sessions, attend educational conferences and promote the project across the country.</p><p>Meanwhile, the website is free and available, and Merchant hopes anyone interested will make use of it.</p><p>“To me,” she said, “it’s about fun and experiencing beauty together, creating community and lifting self-esteem.”</p>

entries.title: Man accused of fatally stabbing woman in Little Village
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago man was charged with fatally stabbing a woman Tuesday in a Little Village apartment. </p><p>David Wilcox, 59, was arrested minutes after the attack and charged with first degree murder, Chicago police said. </p><p>Officers found Wilcox and the woman when they responded to a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/19/woman-killed-man-seriously-injured-in-south-lawndale-stabbing" target="_blank" >report of a person stabbed</a> around 11:35 p.m. in the 2500 block of South Christiana Avenue., police said.</p><p>The 61-year-old woman, who hasn’t yet been identified, suffered multiple puncture wounds and was pronounced dead at the scene, police said.</p><p>At least one steak knife was recovered at the scene, according to a police report, which also stated that the man attacked the woman before stabbing himself.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/11/18/18386589/four-charged-in-carjacking-of-man-taunted-with-don-t-vote-trump" target="_blank" >Wilcox made news in 2016, </a>a day after the Presidential election when he was pulled from a vehicle on the city's West Side as attackers allegedly yelled 'You voted Trump?' </p><p>Court records show that Wilcox was accused of murder in 1986, a charge that was later changed to manslaughter. </p><p>Court information for Wilcox wasn’t immediately available. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Woman critically injured in Garfield Park hit-and-run
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for a vehicle that ran into a woman and left the scene late Thursday in the Garfield Park neighborhood. </p><p>The woman was found unresponsive with trauma to her body in the 3800 block of West Van Buren Street around 11:55 p.m. Thursday, Chicago police said. </p><p>Preliminary information indicates she was struck by a vehicle that left the scene, officials said. </p><p>She was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital where she was in critical condition, police said. </p><p>The Major Accident Investigation Unit is investigating.</p>
